It depends a lot on the conditions -

* Wind - the bigger the tailwind, the faster a road bike is because of tires. With a strong headwind, tires make almost no difference, but a road bike is still faster because it and its rider are more aerodynamic.

* Steepness of grade - the steeper a hill is up or down, the less difference tires make. Very steep uphills almost all pedaling effort goes into overcoming gravity, and very steep downhills friction from tires is insignificant compared to acceleration from gravity and the rotational momentum of the wheels.

So on a flat road or gently uphill or downhill road with no wind or a tailwind, slick tires are significantly faster; in the mountains, there is less of a difference.

But another thing to consider is the impact of riding knobby tires on the road on your wallet - pavement is like sandpaper to soft compound tires, and they will last a fraction of the time compared to keeping them just for off-road riding.

It was much tougher than I thought it would be with much more climbing, and I had no energy at all. It kept climbing up the hillside to where there was snow and ice and then back to the valley bottom. After a landslip the path got very narrow and rocky compared to the previous 4wd tracks. Because I was so tired I couldn't ride the bike properly, and I fell off sideways down the mountainside about 6-7 metres. But I was lucky because I was OK, I didn't even get a bruise from it. I climbed back up to the path and kept going, but it was getting really dark and I realised I still had a long way to go, 5km at least. I was so tired I just wanted to lie down on the ground. It's actually a little complicated (but only takes about 10 seconds with practice) and I believe it only works in the 3-door coupe version, not the 5-door, though I am sure there are other hatchback coupes this would work with:

Slide the passenger seat forward if it isn't already and fold the seats, open the boot/trunk. Stand behind the boot/trunk on the driver's side of the car with the bike on the passenger side (this sounds pedantic but if you don't get this part right, like you're on the wrong side of the bike, it doesn't work).

Lift the bike up with both hands, the rear hand on the seat tube is the best place to grab, lift the front wheel over the boot lid and then you do a bunch of stuff at the same time - twist the handlebars towards you a bit so they clear the hatchback entrance, lean the bike over on its side with the wheels towards the passenger side, lift the rear end of the bike up to clear the chainring and push it forwards. Usually have to shuffle it forwards a couple of times unless it's something small and light like a road bike. With my old downhill bike, it was easiest if the front seat was folded too.

Repeat with the second bike (load the biggest/heaviest bike first and put a blanket over it to protect the paint). Unloading is easier. Reasons for not getting a suspension fork:

* At this budget, a suspension fork means big compromises to the rest of the spec, e.g. lower quality drivetrain and other parts

* At this budget, you can only get low-quality forks from lesser-known brands that a lot of people prefer rigid to.

* At this budget suspension forks add 2-3kg weight to the bike

* It's very hard to run a front rack with a suspension fork

* If you are riding on rocky/bumpy terrain at a speed where you actually need a suspension fork to stay in control of the bike, you are probably going to break your rear wheel or rear rack.

* Rigid forks are almost infinitely less likely to go wrong while on a tour, especially compared to low-quality forks.

A lot of people are suggesting tools that are nice to have and essential if you were fixing bikes for a living, but are certainly not a 'bare minimum requirement' for a home mechanic.

- Chain whip - There are ways to hold the cassette solid without a chain whip. For me, it's not worth it for the once a year I'd use it, and I'd rather practice the no-whip method so I have it down for if I need to change the cassette on a tour.

- Workstand - Nice to have, but certainly not essential.

- Truing stand - I would say this is specialized/trade level equipment and pretty much the opposite of a bare minimum. Truing isn't something you need to do unless you have a problem with your wheel or want to build one - it's possible you could buy it and never use it. You can true OK with the wheels still on the bike using zip ties around the stays/fork legs as guides. You can also make your own truing stand very cheaply/easily - I have one from forks with broken steerer and another with the rear triangle of a broken frame. Truing is also quite an art and is not as simple as other kinds of bicycle maintenance - people are more often happy to leave it to professionals than other jobs.

- Large adjustable wrench - This is useful on old bikes for stuff like threaded headset adjustment, but I'm not clear where you'd use it on a good quality modern bike with press-fit bottom bracket and threadless headset. I can't think of a single thing you'd use it for.

- Snips/cable cutters - This is worth getting as ordinary pliers do a terrible job at cutting cables, but if you already have a high-speed rotary tool, use a cutoff wheel with that instead. I would say it's very rare to need to replace rims that often. Plenty of stories of people getting 15,000 miles out of rims. It depends on the conditions you ride in and if you clean your pads. Riding with a bunch of grit embedded in your pads, or riding with pads worn down to the metal will wear out rims at a highly accelerated rate. Accelerated wear is more of a problem on mountain bikes with rim brakes than on road bikes with rim brakes, as they more often get grit on the braking surface.

Most good quality rims have a small pit or groove in the braking surface; when that is gone, then it's time to replace the rims.

Bear in mind that disc brake pads are usually more expensive than rim brake pads, like $30 vs $15 per wheel at a local bike shop for equivalent quality, and tend to wear faster - for me, it's been more expensive running discs due to this. Rotors also wear away like rims do and have to be replaced - which, while cheaper than wheels, still aren't cheap. You also have to buy a bleed kit to service disc brakes if they're hydraulic, or pay your local bike shop $40 a wheel to bleed them every time they play up, though this is not an issue with cable discs.

How high should my handlebars be in comparison to my seat?

This depends on your flexibility, core strength, and how hard you pedal on average.

It's not as simple as higher handlebars equating to more comfort. For very short rides, that is generally true for everyone, but if you want to ride longer distances, it's usually not the case.

Higher handlebars shift weight off your core, arms, and legs (from the power you put into pedaling) and onto your lower back and seat.

For some riders, this is beneficial, but for those with decent core strength and fitness levels, being too upright can lead to back and butt pain and makes it difficult to exert as much power into the pedals. This can prevent them from covering the same distances they would with lower handlebars.

It's common for newer riders to start with high handlebars and lower them as they gain strength and fitness.

When riding, when should I be using the top of the handlebars and when should I drop down?

The general school of thought is:

The flat part of the handlebars is used to change positions when climbing. The drops are primarily for descending and for situations where you might need to brake hard suddenly (like riding along a busy shopping area or past a school when children are leaving), and sometimes to get out of headwinds. The rest of the time, you should be riding on the brake hoods.

If you find yourself wanting to use the flat part of the handlebars regularly and the hoods are uncomfortable, the bike is likely set up too long for you.
